The result is one of the most hauntingly lyrical dramas in the American canon transformed into a blunt dysfunctional family play in which indelible melancholy gets trampled by anger and bitterness.

But a strategy that might illuminate other dramas disregards the fact that these embellishments — the harmonies of the language, the melodic accents, the music of nostalgia — are intrinsic to the writer's plays, and especially to an intimate “memory play” like this one.
Mr. Gold and his cast, led by an intrepid Sally Field, have dismantled a venerable classic, but darned if they can figure out how to put it back together again.

Instead, in this raw, crisp, and haunting piece of theater, just as Williams intended, there remains for Tom and the other Wingfields just shards—of glass animals, rainbows, and a yearning for connection when all around is torn and unrooted.
The rare revival that breathes new life into a classic rather than defaulting to convention, this Menagerie is well worth another look.
It's a daring, masterful stroke, and one that redefines the Williams classic, and will influence every 'Menagerie' to come in the next few years.

Gold puts his stamp on “Menagerie” with both hyper-realistic elements and a minimalist set so barren it can only leave us to focus on the actors—the juxtaposition of styles makes this “Menagerie” as interesting as any I’ve seen.

Such a defamiliarising approach to classical theatre is perhaps becoming a little too familiar. And yet its virtues are manifest during the play's candlelit final scenes, which hum with ghostly intensity.

This is not a “Glass Menagerie” for everyone, as you will no doubt surmise.
Gold's bare-stage approach puts the focus on fine performances from the central trio.
But overall Gold has given us more of an in-your-face production in which one has to search for snatches of William’s poetry.
This version is neither poetic or expressive, but boring, miscast and missing to what Tennessee Williams intended.

And although the casting is curious, Andrew Lieberman’s set can be confusing, and too much of the staging is head-scratching, it mostly works, resulting in a fresh take on Williams’s most intimate and autobiographical play and the one that put him on the map.

You may surmise that I am less than impressed with the pretentious minimalism that Gold decided to burden a play that needs to float in a sea of clouds and memories and not look like an informal first reading/walkthrough of a play that had never seen the light of day.
Gold made a noble risk that unfortunately didn’t pay off this time.
This Glass Menagerie seems more like a first week’s dress rehearsal than a full-fledged production, lacking the polish needed to make the classic truly shine.

cn.t: Sam Gold's polarizing minimalist revival divides critics sharply. Admirers praise Field's performance and the bold stripped-down approach, while detractors find it misconceived and devoid of Williams' poetry and magic.

vs.sum: The Belasco Theatre offers stunning ambiance with its historic Tiffany lamps and stained-glass ceiling, but suffers from tight legroom typical of older venues. While sound quality is generally good, sightlines can be inconsistent, especially from side orchestra seats.
